title: Clinical restoration of a complete human skin organ

concept.text: The innovation would restore the structure and working functions of adult human skin across clinically meaningful full-thickness wounds after burns, trauma or surgical excision. It would recreate a stable epidermal barrier, organized underlying dermis and anatomically appropriate appendages, such as hair follicles and glands, together with the vascular and sensory integration needed for durable function. The goal extends beyond closing a wound: ordinary deep adult wounds generally heal through fibrosis without rebuilding the original architecture and appendages.

Two alternative routes belong within this capability: inducing the patient's wound to regenerate skin in place, or producing an engineered skin organ and transplanting it. Patient-specific bioengineered skin is the graft route within DER-01, rather than a separate innovation. Clinical-scale manufacture is a requirement for that route; endogenous regeneration would instead require reliable control of tissue rebuilding throughout the wound. This is a proposed capability, and neither route is established by the supplied evidence as a durable, complete solution for adult human full-thickness skin loss.

Restoration must respect the body site. Hair follicles are appropriate in haired skin, but should not be required in normally hairless, or glabrous, skin. Likewise, appendage composition and functional targets should reflect local anatomy. Early fetal scar-free healing provides a biological precedent for regenerative repair, but its developmental restriction is more complex than a capacity simply lost at birth: outcomes vary with developmental stage, wound size and depth.

significance.text: Successful restoration would change the outcome of major skin loss from scar-based repair toward reconstruction of a functioning organ. Scarred skin generally has reduced tensile strength and resilience and lacks normal appendage architecture. Recreating dermal organization and functional appendages could therefore address structural deficits that wound coverage alone leaves behind. Sensory recovery is a separate outcome to measure; the evidence does not justify treating every scar as entirely insensate.

Conditional impact synthesis: a treatment that reliably restored these structures and functions over substantial wounds could improve recovery after burns, trauma and excision and reduce the lasting burden of scar-based reconstruction. An engineered graft would be especially consequential if it could integrate with the recipient's circulation and nerves while maintaining the appendages appropriate to the site. These benefits depend on demonstrated function and durability, rather than on skin-like appearance alone.

Normal pigmentation, effective temperature regulation and extensive sensory recovery would broaden the achievement, but would not follow automatically from finding two appendage types and some sensation in a treated area. The 2020 skin-organoid report describes sensory neurons, Schwann cells and nerve-like bundles targeting Merkel cells in follicles; this supplies a technical basis for pursuing sensory constructs, but neural architecture alone does not demonstrate normal sensation in a human graft. Similarly, gland formation must be distinguished from effective sweating and thermoregulation.

Conditional translation synthesis: patient-derived grafts could offer a route to individualized reconstruction, but immune compatibility, safe cell production and affordable manufacture would still need demonstration. Growth with a child's body would be an additional pediatric achievement requiring longitudinal evidence. Neither autologous origin nor successful initial engraftment establishes these outcomes. Distal fingertip regeneration and fetal-like skin organoids are useful precedents, but their restricted anatomy and developmental state limit the analogy to general adult skin restoration.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is coordinated rebuilding of epidermis, organized dermis and appropriate appendages across a clinically meaningful adult human full-thickness defect, with sustained function. Ordinary fibrotic repair can reestablish a protective barrier while failing to restore the original tissue architecture. Regenerative treatment must therefore change how the wound is rebuilt, rather than merely accelerate closure or reduce the visible scar.

Biological barriers include coordinating epithelial–mesenchymal interactions and developmental signaling so that follicles and glands form in the right tissue context while dermal repair avoids a persistently fibrotic structure. Mouse wound-induced hair follicle neogenesis shows that appendage formation can occur during adult mammalian repair, but transferring that result to human wounds remains unresolved. Follicle reconstruction also requires maturation and sustained growth cycles: producing a follicle-shaped structure or an initial hair is insufficient evidence of a durable replacement.

For engineered grafts, the barriers include suitable and reproducible cell sources, retention of regenerative competence, maturation beyond fetal-like tissue, vascular integration, functional innervation and consistent appendage production. Chu and colleagues describe cell-source restrictions on standardized manufacture, difficulty reproducing embryonic signals and sustaining follicle cycling, and substantial cost, time, variability and safety concerns around patient-specific organoid production. These are obstacles to reliable clinical manufacture, rather than evidence that no appendage-bearing constructs have been made.

Engineering synthesis: the remaining integration problem is to make these components work together throughout a substantial wound and remain stable over years. A usable treatment must couple tissue architecture with perfusion, protective sensation and site-appropriate appendage function, while controlling adverse growth, immune complications and recurrent fibrosis. Large-area delivery, production consistency and cost require route-specific solutions. The supplied reviews document these broad challenges but do not establish an exhaustive absence of complete-skin manufacturing as of November 1, 2026.

current_state.text: The supplied clinical-gap evidence includes two full-text reviews. Frech and Lichtenberger's February 16, 2024 review identifies restoration of fully functional skin and dermal appendages as an unmet goal and distinguishes barrier repair from recovery of original architecture. Yang, Liu and Cheng's October 22, 2025 review describes the failure of ordinary scar healing to regenerate glands and hair follicles and the continuing lack of a clinical method for scar-free healing. Together they support a substantial gap between wound closure and complete functional restoration, while allowing for experimental regenerative results and restricted exceptions.

NIAMS identifies skin regeneration and scalable, economical production of complex tissues as priorities in its fiscal years 2025–2029 strategic plan. The page recorded in the supplied review was last updated in April 2025; the earlier research notes' December 2024 date was not confirmed. The plan establishes an institutional research direction, rather than a completed restoration method or a comprehensive inventory of available therapies.

Schultz and colleagues' November 5, 2025 paper reports semi-occlusive treatment of fingertip amputations in 22 patients aged 2–72 years, with treatment conducted during 2017–2019. The authors characterize distal fingertip restoration as a possible example of human epimorphic regeneration. This is a restricted human precedent, rather than evidence of large-area restoration of ordinary haired or glabrous skin. Histological blastema formation remains unproven, and the supplied review did not visually inspect the figures or supplements.

Large adult mouse wounds can generate new hair follicles, as reviewed by Frech and Lichtenberger; their discussion includes increased central wound follicle neogenesis with epidermal Wnt7a overexpression. Experimental manipulation of regenerative signaling, including YAP-related approaches, is also discussed in the supplied reviews. These are animal precedents rather than human demonstrations. The earlier blanket description of YAP blockade as a mouse result needs qualification because Yang and colleagues describe a cited model as rat. The supplied review provides secondary-source support for these experiments, without independent inspection of their primary experimental figures.

Xiong and colleagues' 2024 Advanced Materials abstract reports a cell-free approach to antiscar healing with regeneration of hair follicles, sebaceous glands and sweat glands, while presenting clinical applications and burn rehabilitation as future potential. The accessible evidence in the supplied review is the PubMed abstract record. The abstract does not identify the experimental species, although the record includes a Mice indexing term. That indexing does not establish the full experimental design; methods, wound scale, durability and figures were unavailable for assessment. These access limits restrict interpretation without establishing that the reported result is false.

Lee, Koehler and colleagues' June 3, 2020 Nature report describes human pluripotent-stem-cell-derived skin organoids resembling second-trimester fetal facial skin and planar hair-bearing skin after grafting onto nude mice. The abstract also reports sensory neurons and Schwann cells forming nerve-like bundles associated with follicular Merkel cells. The supplied review had a subscription preview, supplementary information and a reporting summary, rather than the full main article; images were not inspected. The supplementary discussion describes the hairs as lanugo-like rather than vellus or terminal and leaves anatomical identity uncertain. This is an important preclinical construct result, with developmental and transplantation limits that prevent equating it with mature, clinically scaled human skin replacement.

Chu and colleagues' February 21, 2025 review describes substantial progress in follicle reconstruction alongside continuing difficulties with embryonic signaling, sustained growth cycles, cell sources, maturation, safety and manufacture. Yang and colleagues distinguish wound-covering products from permanent replacement and discuss vascularization and appendage barriers. Cultured epidermal sheets can provide wound coverage and epidermal continuity, but those achievements do not by themselves establish an organized, appendage-bearing and functionally integrated full-thickness skin organ.

Evidence-scope synthesis: the supplied material supports these dated findings, but contains no bounded search establishing comprehensive field status through November 1, 2026. It therefore supports a documented restoration gap without proving that no additional clinical development or manufacturing capability exists. The uncaptured Lee scalp immune-cell attribution and the uncaptured 2026 translational extract are not needed to establish that gap and cannot strengthen it without further verification.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed human demonstration: prospectively treat clinically meaningful full-thickness wounds or burn excisions and show a stable epidermal barrier, dermal collagen organization approaching the basket-weave pattern of uninjured skin, and functional, anatomically appropriate appendages. Compare treated tissue with the patient's uninjured skin and with standard graft or scar outcomes. The proposal to require at least two appendage types should apply only where appropriate to the site's normal anatomy; glabrous skin needs its own criteria. These are proposed demonstration requirements, rather than established clinical standards.
completion_criteria.label: Human full-thickness wounds regain barrier, dermal architecture and functional appendages

completion_criteria.text: The scientific basis for assessing both architecture and function is the distinction between barrier closure and original tissue restoration. Yang and colleagues describe basket-weave collagen organization in normal tissue versus more parallel collagen alignment after injury, while Frech and Lichtenberger describe the architectural and mechanical deficits of scar. Chu and colleagues' discussion of sustained follicle cycling supports testing durable appendage function rather than relying on a single morphological observation.
completion_criteria.label: Assessment distinguishes tissue restoration from closure through architecture and function

completion_criteria.text: Proposed quantitative protocol: specify wound area and depth, the fraction of treated tissue meeting structural targets, appendage density and distribution, appendage-specific functional tests, and sensory thresholds over a predefined fraction of the wound or graft. Assess protective sensation directly rather than inferring it from nerve staining. Evaluate barrier performance and mechanical integrity alongside histology. Candidate follow-up points are one year and again after several years, with precise intervals and acceptable outcomes defined before treatment. The supplied evidence does not establish numerical cutoffs for these measures.
completion_criteria.label: Predefined protocols quantify structural and functional restoration across treated wounds

completion_criteria.text: Proposed graft-route demonstration: produce reproducible patient-derived tissue that becomes adequately vascularized and functionally innervated before or after transplantation and maintains its structure and function for years. Demonstrate manufacturing consistency, feasible production time and cost, immune compatibility and long-term safety at the intended treatment area. Normal pigmentation, effective thermoregulation and growth with a child's body require additional targeted testing if claimed; meeting the minimum structural and partial sensory criteria would not establish them.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible patient-derived grafts maintain integrated structure and function for years

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scope requirements: reproduce outcomes across patients and, where feasible, independent clinical teams, with predefined failure and safety endpoints. Report the wound sizes, anatomical sites, patient characteristics and treatment routes actually tested. A mouse graft, a fingertip injury result or an epidermal sheet alone would not meet the proposed adult full-thickness organ-restoration bar. Successful finite trials would establish restoration within the demonstrated settings, rather than literal universality across all wounds, body sites or populations.
completion_criteria.label: Restoration reproduces across patients with reported scope and predefined endpoints

related_concepts.text: Roster-based scope synthesis — DER-02, One-time genomic cure of severe monogenic skin disease through the epidermal stem-cell compartment: both concepts may use patient-derived cells and transplantation, but DER-02 requires durable correction of a disease-causing genotype in the renewing epidermis. DER-01 requires reconstruction of full-thickness architecture and function after tissue loss. A genetically corrected epidermal graft could contribute to a combined treatment without, by itself, satisfying complete skin-organ restoration.

Roster-based scope synthesis — DER-03, Antigen-selective erasure of pathogenic cutaneous immune memory, and DER-07, A skin-origin intervention that prevents atopic dermatitis and the atopic march: these target distinct immune and disease-prevention outcomes. Immune control may help reconstructed skin survive or function, but restoration of tissue architecture does not establish selective immune-memory erasure or prevention of downstream allergic disease.

Roster-based scope synthesis — DER-04, Programmable passage of macromolecules and gene editors across intact stratum corneum: this is a delivery capability that might support regenerative interventions where an intact barrier must be crossed. DER-01 concerns rebuilding missing tissue. Successful delivery does not demonstrate organ restoration, and a graft or open-wound regenerative treatment need not solve delivery across intact skin.

Roster-based scope synthesis — DER-05, Epidermal DNA repair sufficient to prevent ultraviolet-driven skin cancer, and DER-06, Therapeutic reset of the mutant epidermal field: these concern genome protection or management of mutation-bearing epidermis. They may share cell-engineering or replacement techniques with DER-01, but a restored skin organ does not automatically repair ultraviolet damage, remove a mutant field or prevent cancer. Conversely, those epidermal interventions need not recreate dermis, glands or follicles.

Roster-based scope synthesis — DER-08, Reconstitution of melanocyte stem cells where the follicular reservoir is gone: follicle reconstruction and pigmentation could overlap with complete skin restoration, but DER-08 focuses on restoring a specific stem-cell population after loss of its reservoir. Appendage-bearing skin does not automatically demonstrate a durable melanocyte reservoir or normal pigmentation, and melanocyte restoration alone does not establish complete skin-organ reconstruction.

Roster-based scope synthesis — DER-09, Durable regenerative closure of diabetic foot ulcers after ischemia and pressure are treated: the concepts overlap in regenerative wound treatment, but DER-09 has a specific clinical setting and requires durable closure after vascular and mechanical contributors are addressed. DER-01 sets a broader architectural and functional reconstruction target. Closure of a diabetic ulcer does not automatically establish complete organ restoration, while restoration in another wound population would not establish effectiveness in diabetic foot ulcers.

Roster-based scope synthesis — DER-10, In situ reversal of established keloids and pathological cutaneous scars: both concepts may involve modifying fibrosis, but DER-10 treats an existing pathological scar. DER-01 concerns restoration across a full-thickness defect through regeneration or grafting. Preventing a new scar, reversing an established scar and rebuilding missing appendages are distinguishable achievements; success in one does not establish the others.

change_log.change: Preserved DER-01 and its title, and integrated endogenous regeneration and patient-specific engineered grafts as alternative routes to the same capability.
change_log.reason: The concept's identity is organ-level restoration; the route of treatment does not justify splitting or deleting it.

change_log.change: Replaced the claim that scar-free repair is lost after birth with a developmental, wound-size and wound-depth qualification.
change_log.reason: The reviewed evidence describes prenatal transitions and context-dependent healing rather than a single birth boundary.

change_log.change: Qualified universal statements about adult wounds, scar sensation and the absence of complete-skin manufacturing.
change_log.reason: The sources support general fibrotic repair and a substantial restoration gap, but not universal sensory loss or an exhaustive manufacturing absence through November 1, 2026.

change_log.change: Separated architectural restoration, anatomical innervation and demonstrated sensory function, and made appendage requirements site-specific.
change_log.reason: Nerve-like structures do not establish normal sensation, and hair follicles are inappropriate requirements for normally glabrous skin.

change_log.change: Retained pigmentation, thermoregulation, pediatric growth, affordability and immune compatibility as additional outcomes or translation requirements.
change_log.reason: These important possibilities exceed what follows from two appendage types and partial sensory recovery.

change_log.change: Expanded the fingertip account with 22 patients, ages 2–72, treatment during 2017–2019, the November 5, 2025 publication date and the unproven blastema limitation.
change_log.reason: These details preserve the human result while defining its anatomical scope and evidentiary limits.

change_log.change: Retained mouse follicle neogenesis while qualifying the species attribution of YAP-related experiments.
change_log.reason: Mouse follicle neogenesis has review-level support, but the supplied reviews do not support a blanket mouse designation for all cited YAP work.

change_log.change: Expanded the Xiong account to distinguish the abstract's appendage claims, future clinical application and Mice indexing from unavailable experimental methods.
change_log.reason: Indexing alone cannot resolve species, wound scale or durability, and incomplete access does not establish that the result is false.

change_log.change: Integrated the organoid study's fetal facial-skin resemblance, neural architecture, lanugo-like hairs and uncertain anatomical identity.
change_log.reason: These useful scientific distinctions explain both the achievement and the developmental gap to mature human skin replacement.

change_log.change: Clarified that the Nature evidence comprised a subscription preview, supplementary information and a reporting summary rather than the full main article.
change_log.reason: Artifact labels could otherwise imply broader access than the supplied review actually had.

change_log.change: Corrected the NIAMS date to the reviewed page's April 2025 update and retained the distinction between research priorities and completed methods.
change_log.reason: The supplied review did not confirm the earlier December 2024 date.

change_log.change: Withheld the uncaptured scalp γδ T-cell attribution and the claimed 2026 translational extract as substantive support.
change_log.reason: Neither attribution was verifiable in the supplied review; independently reviewed sources still support the central restoration gap.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed demonstration to include quantified tissue coverage, appendage function, sensory testing, reproducibility and bounded clinical generalization.
change_log.reason: The original criteria were coherent proposals but lacked operational thresholds and could otherwise imply that a minimum demonstration establishes every skin function.

change_log.change: Explained overlap and distinctions with every other supplied roster entry.
change_log.reason: Shared technologies do not merge their distinct biological and clinical objectives.

unresolved_issues: No bounded freshness search is supplied, so comprehensive clinical and manufacturing status through November 1, 2026 remains unresolved.

The Lee claim concerning dermal γδ T cells in human scalp and the 2026 translational-review extract remain unverified because their sources were not captured. Their omission as supporting evidence is not a finding that they are false.

Precise species and experimental attribution for individual YAP-blockade results require primary-source clarification; the supplied reviews include a rat-model description alongside the earlier mouse characterization.
For Xiong and colleagues, the abstract and Mice indexing do not resolve the full experimental design, wound dimensions, durability or translational boundaries.
The Nature main article was not available in full to the supplied review, and images were not inspected. Its supplement supports lanugo-like hair and leaves anatomical identity uncertain.
The fingertip study does not establish histological blastema formation or general restoration of large areas of ordinary skin.

Minimum wound area, appendage density and function, sensory thresholds, safety limits and exact long-term follow-up intervals remain to be specified. The suggested two-appendage and follow-up requirements are proposals, not consensus standards.
Normal pigmentation, effective thermoregulation, extensive sensory recovery, pediatric growth and affordable large-area manufacture require separate demonstrations.

brief.title: Restoring fully working skin after deep wounds
possible: After a severe burn, injury or surgery, people could regain skin with its protective surface, supporting inner layer, working glands and hair where it belongs. Blood vessels and nerves would connect the rebuilt tissue to the body.
Treatment could help skin regrow directly in a wound or replace lost skin with tissue grown from the patient's own cells.
why: Deep wounds usually heal with scars that lack the strength, flexibility and structures of uninjured skin. Restoring working skin could improve recovery and reduce the lasting burden of reconstruction for people with major skin loss.

sources.who: Wenhui Yang, Liu Liu and Xingjian Cheng
sources.showed: Their review describes how ordinary healing leaves scars without restored glands or hair follicles, and examines experimental ways to change that outcome.
sources.quote: Additionally, skin appendages, such as glands and hair follicles, do not regenerate
sources.cited_for: Closing a wound does not restore all the structures of healthy skin.
sources.not_established: The review does not demonstrate a treatment that restores complete, lasting skin function in deep human wounds.

sources.who: Sophie Frech and Beate M. Lichtenberger
sources.showed: Their review describes new hair formation in large animal wounds and how signals between cells might shift healing toward rebuilding skin.
sources.quote: Only in rabbits and mice with large injuries HF neogenesis has been described in adult tissues
sources.cited_for: Adult mammals can rebuild hair follicles, the structures that grow hair, within some wounds.
sources.not_established: Animal hair regrowth does not establish complete skin restoration in adult human wounds.

sources.who: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases
sources.showed: Its research plan prioritizes skin regeneration and affordable ways to produce complex replacement tissues.
sources.cited_for: Skin regeneration and production of replacement tissue are institutional research priorities.
sources.not_established: A research priority does not demonstrate a working treatment.

sources.showed: They treated fingertip amputations in 22 patients with silicone caps and reported regrowth of skin, nailbed and tissue beneath the skin.
sources.quote: In all patients, subcutaneous tissue, nailbed and skin regenerated with excellent outcomes.
sources.cited_for: Human fingertips provide a restricted example of tissue regrowth after injury.
sources.not_established: This small study does not establish restoration across large wounds or other body sites.

sources.showed: They reported an artificial skin material that reduced scarring and supported regrowth of hair follicles, oil glands and sweat glands without transplanted cells.
sources.quote: Therefore, the RDAS offers a cell-free antiscarring therapeutic strategy for regenerative wound healing, resulting in improved outcomes.
sources.cited_for: A material applied to wounds can support experimental regrowth of several skin structures.
sources.not_established: The result does not establish durable restoration of substantial adult human wounds, with working nerves and blood supply.

sources.who: Jiyoon Lee, Karl R. Koehler and colleagues
sources.showed: They grew small skin tissues from human stem cells, cells able to form different tissues. These contained hair follicles, oil glands and nerve-like bundles, and formed flat, hair-bearing skin on mice.
sources.quote: Moreover, we show that skin organoids form planar hair-bearing skin when grafted onto nude mice.
sources.cited_for: Human cells can assemble complex skin tissue that survives transplantation onto mice.
sources.not_established: The tissue resembled fetal skin; mature function, normal sensation and lasting replacement of human wounds remain unproven.

sources.showed: Their review describes progress in rebuilding hair follicles and continuing problems with cell sources, development and repeated hair growth.
sources.cited_for: A rebuilt follicle must mature and sustain hair growth cycles to provide lasting replacement.
sources.not_established: Follicle reconstruction alone does not establish a complete skin replacement that can be produced reliably for patients.

shown: Lee, Koehler and colleagues grew complex human skin tissue with hair follicles, oil glands and nerve-like bundles, then transplanted it onto mice. It resembled fetal skin. Schultz and colleagues reported tissue regrowth in human fingertips, a limited anatomical setting.
missing: A treatment has yet to demonstrate lasting restoration of all skin layers and appropriate glands and hair across substantial deep adult human wounds.
Rebuilt skin needs a working blood supply, protective sensation and sustained gland and hair function throughout the treated area.
Patient-derived replacement skin needs reliable production at a useful scale, with demonstrated safety, immune compatibility and feasible cost.

milestones.label: Deep human wounds regain working skin
milestones.explanation: Treated deep human wounds would have to regain a stable barrier, normally organized supporting tissue and working glands and hair appropriate to the site. This would demonstrate rebuilding beyond scar-based repair.

milestones.label: Assessment separates restored skin from wound closure
milestones.explanation: Assessment would have to distinguish normal tissue organization and lasting gland and hair function from simple wound closure. This would prevent a healed surface from counting as a restored organ.

milestones.label: Predefined tests measure restoration across the wound
milestones.explanation: Tests set before treatment would have to measure structure, coverage, barrier strength, gland and hair function, and sensation across the wound over time. This would establish how much skin actually works.

milestones.label: Patient-derived replacement skin works reliably for years
milestones.explanation: Skin grown from patients' cells would have to be produced consistently, connect to blood vessels and nerves, and work safely for years at feasible cost. This would establish a usable transplant route.

milestones.label: Restoration repeats across patients
milestones.explanation: Results would have to repeat across patients and, where feasible, clinical teams, using predefined success and safety measures. Reporting wound types and body sites would establish where treatment works.

uncertain: The minimum wound size, extent of restoration, acceptable sensation and duration of follow-up needed to count as success remain unsettled.
It remains unclear how reliably animal wound regrowth and fetal-like human skin tissue can translate into mature skin restoration in adults.
Normal skin colour, effective sweating, extensive sensory recovery and growth with a child's body each require separate demonstration.

page.title: Full-thickness human skin regeneration
page.definition: Adult full-thickness skin loss is replaced by epidermis, the surface barrier, and dermis, the supporting connective tissue, with site-appropriate hair follicles and glands, blood supply and sensation. Restoration can occur within the wound or through transplantation of engineered skin.

goal.need: WHO estimated 163,000 deaths worldwide from fire, heat and hot substances in 2023. Survivors can require repeated surgery and rehabilitation. In a denovoSkin burn study, 15 grafted participants had a mean burn extent of 46% of total body surface area. The study measured coverage obtained per unit of donor skin, a constraint when treating extensive burns.

figures.caption: Wound coverage obtained per unit of harvested donor skin
figures.note: Ratios are cm² of grafted area with take per cm² of harvested donor skin, measured four weeks after grafting in 15 participants.

statements.body: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases
statements.quote: Identifying and characterizing new genetic, molecular, and cellular mechanisms that drive and restrain musculoskeletal, cartilage, and skin regeneration.
statements.context: A research priority in the strategic plan for fiscal years 2025–2029.

statements.quote: restoration of the skin’s normal architecture, lack of fibrosis and regeneration of skin appendages – hair follicles, sebaceous glands and eccrine glands.
statements.context: The public abstract of funded University of Southern California disease-team planning award DT1-00653 describes its intended regenerative wound-healing outcome.

completion.title: An adult full-thickness wound regains skin architecture and site-appropriate physiological functions.
completion.criterion: A peer-reviewed clinical study in adults with full-thickness skin loss demonstrates epidermis and dermis with normal architecture, barrier and mechanical function, perfusion, protective sensation, and functioning appendages appropriate to the treated site. Appendage tests demonstrate hair cycling, sebum secretion and sweating wherever those functions normally occur. Closure meets the FDA definition and remains intact during at least 3 months of follow-up after closure.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback, combining NIAMS and CIRM regeneration goals with FDA wound-closure criteria.
completion.basis: Searches of NIAMS and CIRM goals, FDA wound guidance, EMA tissue-engineering guidance, ISO/ASTM standards and prize criteria found no combined clinical test of complete skin restoration. This fallback retains the stated structural and functional goal and FDA closure criteria. The 2019 single-patient report assessed follicles and touch but supplied no direct sweating or repeated hair-cycling test.

milestones.title: Human skin organoids form layered skin, hair follicles and sebaceous glands by about day 130.
milestones.criterion: Human pluripotent stem cells produce skin organoids containing stratified skin layers, pigmented hair follicles, sebaceous glands, Merkel cells and sensory neurons at approximately 130 days of differentiation. The published protocol describes tissue resembling human fetal skin at 18 weeks of gestation. Merkel cells are touch-associated epithelial cells. This benchmark concerns laboratory tissue formation.
milestones.set_by: Lee and colleagues, the published Nature Protocols skin-organoid protocol of 23 March 2022. The benchmark was developed for hair-bearing, fetal-like skin.
milestones.threshold_quote: By day ~130, the skin organoids reach full complexity and contain stratified skin layers, pigmented hair follicles, sebaceous glands

milestones.title: Engineered dermal–epidermal skin is transplanted into people with skin defects of at least 9 cm².
milestones.criterion: People with deep partial-thickness or full-thickness defects requiring surgical coverage receive an engineered dermal–epidermal graft under an authorized first-in-human protocol. NCT02145130 specified defects of at least 9 cm² and replacement products of 9–49 cm². Its denovoSkin cohort comprised 10 treated children, with safety and graft take assessed during the clinical phase.
milestones.set_by: University of Zurich, first-in-human protocol NCT02145130, authorized by Ethics Committee Zurich on 29 January 2013. Its size criteria concern the denovoSkin and denovoDerm graft programme.
milestones.threshold_quote: These skin replacement products will be transplanted in sizes ranging from 9 to 49 cm2.

milestones.title: Treated human wounds close without drainage or dressings at visits two weeks apart.
milestones.criterion: The wound is completely re-epithelialized, with no drainage or dressing requirement, at two consecutive study visits 2 weeks apart. FDA guidance recommends follow-up for at least 3 months after closure to assess durability and adverse effects. The denovoSkin phase IIb study reported 100% epithelialization of experimental and control areas at 3 months in its 15 grafted participants.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, June 2006 guidance, section IV.G.1.a. The definition is stated for chronic nonhealing wounds within guidance covering cutaneous ulcers and burns.
milestones.threshold_quote: without drainage or dressing requirements confirmed at two consecutive study visits 2 weeks apart.

milestones.title: Engineered skin provides more coverage per donor area than split-thickness grafts at day 28.
milestones.criterion: In a randomized within-patient comparison, engineered skin achieves a greater ratio of grafted area with take to harvested donor area at day 28 ± 3, passing the protocol's two-sided significance level of 0.05. NCT03227146 enrolled 21 patients between 26 March 2018 and 26 July 2022 and grafted 15. The reported primary comparison achieved p < 0.001.
milestones.set_by: University of Zurich and collaborating burn centres, denovoSkin phase IIb protocol NCT03227146 and its published statistical analysis. This donor-sparing endpoint concerns the graft route.
milestones.threshold_quote: A claim of study success was to be made when the two-sided test would pass the significance level of 0·05.

milestones.title: Engineered human skin remains intact without clinically detected tumors for five years.
milestones.criterion: Grafted skin retains clinical stability through the assessment at 5 years ± 30 days after transplantation, using the protocol's checks for ulceration, secretion, blistering, skin breakdown and tumor formation. Seven of 10 denovoSkin-treated children completed five-year follow-up. The investigators reported stable grafts and no clinically detected tumors among those assessed.
milestones.set_by: University Children's Hospital Zurich, long-term follow-up protocol NCT02145130. These clinical stability and safety assessments were specified for denovoSkin.
milestones.threshold_quote: continuing until 5 years ± 30 days post-transplantation of denovoSkin (visits 9-13)

milestones.title: An adult full-thickness wound regains hair follicles and measurable touch sensation.
milestones.criterion: A treated adult full-thickness wound contains reconstructed skin with hair follicles and demonstrable touch sensation. A report published on 13 March 2019 described one 31-year-old man treated with an autologous skin construct over 200 cm². Microscopy examined regenerated follicles, static two-point discrimination was assessed at 14 weeks, and wound coverage persisted at 6 months. Direct gland secretion and repeated hair cycling remain unverified.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback based on Granick and colleagues' clinical proof-of-concept assessments. Searches found no registered combined success threshold for appendage-bearing reconstruction and sensory recovery.

not_found: No common numerical cutoffs were found for minimum restored wound area, appendage density, sensory recovery or duration of complete physiological restoration.
FDA two-visit closure confirmation could not be verified from the denovoSkin phase IIb publication.
The CIRM award abstract supplies no publication date.
The supplied Nature main article and several supplied PMC reviews could not be read through the web interface.
EMA's reflection paper on clinical aspects of tissue-engineered products could not be opened.

results.finding: Skin regenerated in all 22 patients with fingertip amputations.
results.detail: The study describes epithelialization but does not establish complete closure without drainage or dressings at two visits two weeks apart.
results.quote: A silicone finger cap, comprising a puncturable reservoir, was used to treat 22 human fingertip amputations. In all patients, subcutaneous tissue, nailbed and skin regenerated with excellent outcomes.

results.finding: Human pluripotent stem cell-derived skin organoids formed hair-bearing layered skin in 4–5 months; overall sample size not stated.
results.detail: The organoids also contained Merkel cells and sensory neurons. The authors compared them with second-trimester fetal facial skin, including 18-week specimens.
results.quote: During an incubation period of 4–5 months, we observe the emergence of a cyst-like skin organoid composed of stratified epidermis, fat-rich dermis and pigmented hair follicles that are equipped with sebaceous glands.

results.finding: In 50 patients treated with an autologous skin construct, 35 diabetic foot ulcers closed by 12 weeks.
results.detail: Closure required complete epithelialization without drainage at two visits two weeks apart, but the study does not state that dressings were unnecessary. The ulcers were superficial, and there was no follow-up beyond the 12-week treatment period.
results.quote: By 12 weeks, there were significantly more wounds closed in the AHSC group (35/50, 70.0%) than in the control group (17/50, 34.0%)

results.finding: Among 52 patients, 65% of areas treated with skin cell suspension and meshed autograft achieved complete closure by week 8.
results.detail: Closure meant complete re-epithelialization without drainage at two visits at least two weeks apart. The study did not establish that dressings were unnecessary; after closure, protection with compression garments or gauze and secondary dressings was used as needed.
results.quote: In the PP population, 30 patients (58%) had complete closure at Control STSG areas compared with 34 patients (65%) at ASCS+STSG areas at Week 8

results.finding: In 15 grafted burn patients, denovoSkin achieved greater donor-area-adjusted coverage than split-thickness grafts at day 28 (p < 0.001).
results.detail: In the randomized within-patient comparison, the median expansion ratio was seven times greater with denovoSkin. The endpoint measured grafted area with take per harvested donor area at day 28 ± 3.
results.quote: The expansion ratio for denovoSkin™ versus STSG was 7·0 times larger for denovoSkin™ (p < 0·001).

results.finding: Among 10 children treated with denovoSkin, 7 completed five-year follow-up with stable grafts and no clinically detected tumors.
results.detail: One of the three children who did not complete follow-up experienced complete graft loss and was re-grafted; the other two discontinued for reasons unrelated to graft stability.
results.quote: Of the 10 patients treated with denovoSkin in this phase I clinical trial, 7 completed the 5-year follow-up period. Skin substitutes continued to be deemed safe, remained stable, and practically unchanged, with no sign of fragility and no tumor formation at clinical examination.
